docs.title: Program Design and Rationale
docs.markdown:
# Program Design and Rationale

## 1. Program Overview

The program runs year-round across five off-season and in-season phases, plus a transition phase (Phase 0) between them:

| Phase | Window | Primary Intent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 — Transition | Monday after the final game through the Sunday before Phase 1 Testing Week | Recovery, then a coach-facilitated on-ramp |
| 1 — Winter | Mid-December – late February | Max strength & hypertrophy |
| 2 — Spring | Early March – late May | Strength-speed & power |
| 3 — Early Summer | Late June – mid July | Speed & conditioning |
| 4 — Pre-Camp Taper | Mid-to-late July | Arrive at camp fresh, not fried |
| 5 — In-Season | Camp through the final regular-season game | Maintain strength/power, manage total weekly load |

The design follows a sequential periodization model: General Physical Preparedness (GPP) in winter builds a broad strength and work-capacity base, which Specific Physical Preparedness (SPP) in spring converts into football-specific power and speed expression, which early summer sharpens into pure speed and conditioning once full days are available. A two-week taper protects that work into camp, and the in-season phase protects what was built without adding to the load practice and games already place on the athletes. This progression — and the underlying idea that trying to develop every athletic quality at once produces worse results than building them in a specific order — reflects established sport-science periodization theory (the NSCA's CSCS periodization chapter; Bompa's framework) and is reinforced throughout by NSCA, NATA, and ASCA position statements on adolescent training, injury prevention, and safe return from inactivity.

Program-design ideas are structurally inspired by John Welbourn's PowerAthlete materials (*Be the Hammer*, *Bedrock*, *Speed Kills*) — primal movement patterns first (squat, lunge, hinge, push, pull, carry), the GPP-to-SPP progression, Compensatory Acceleration Training (CAT), a testing-and-retesting rhythm for auto-regulation, and the "boiling point, not breaking point" principle governing the taper. These are used as philosophical and structural inspiration only, not adopted wholesale: this is a program built for this roster size, this equipment, this coaching staff, and this schedule, and where the literature or this team's actual constraints point a different direction than Welbourn's own programming, the program follows the evidence instead. The clearest example is **Phase 5's in-season lift timing**. Welbourn's *Be the Hammer* schedules the hardest training session for the day after a game, on the reasoning that CNS recovery outpaces muscular recovery — a principle built around NFL-level recovery infrastructure (contrast baths, EMS, controlled nutrition) this program does not have. Muscle-damage markers after a game typically peak 24–48 hours post-contact and can remain incompletely recovered at 48–72 hours, and a GPS-tracked study of in-season college football practice load (Johnson, Yang, Cabarkapa et al., 2025, *Frontiers in Sports and Active Living*) found that teams' own practice schedules already load hardest four days before the next game and lightest the day before it. This program's two weekly lift days sit on the days furthest from the last game and the next one, not immediately after a game, working with that shape rather than against it.

A second divergence worth naming directly: Welbourn's programs assume a positionally undifferentiated roster. This program splits by position group throughout — linemen biased toward the max-strength/heavier-load end of every lane, skill positions biased toward speed and lighter loads moved faster (as written in the phase documents and applied by the coach; the app itself automates only the Phase 1 Jump Station swap by lane, and the ±2.5-percentage-point load bias stays coach judgment, capped at 87% of e1RM in the Phase 1 peak weeks) — because a uniform, velocity-first approach applied to an entire roster has a documented failure mode. In 2021, the University of Texas shifted its off-season program to a velocity-based training model applied uniformly across the roster; its offensive and defensive linemen came out of that off-season weaker, leaner, and slower, and the program corrected back toward traditional max-strength work for its bigger positions the following year. That single documented case — not a controlled study, and treated here descriptively rather than as substitute evidence — is the direct reason this program never applies one training emphasis to every position group.

## 2. Load & Effort Methodology

**Estimated One-Rep Max (e1RM).** Every phase's main-lift loads are prescribed as a percentage of each athlete's **e1RM**, not their raw tested weight. Testing Week (and every retest) has athletes work up to a true 5-rep max (5RM), not a single-rep true 1RM — a 5RM gives a real, usable number with less technique risk, which is a conservative program choice. The NSCA youth statement supports supervised maximal testing after a habituation period; it does not say a 5RM is safer than a 1RM. Immediately after testing, each 5RM is converted once to an estimated 1RM:

**e1RM = tested 5RM ÷ 0.87** (round to the nearest 2.5 lb)

This conversion matters because the program's central research citations — Hoffman & Kang's finding that football players training at ≥80% of pre-season *1RM* had significantly greater in-season strength improvements than those training below 80%, and the CAT literature's 50–70% *1RM* loading range — are expressed in percent-of-true-1RM terms. A 5RM is standardly about 87% of a true 1RM (NSCA %RM table); applying research-derived percentages directly to a raw 5RM would understate true intensity and run training below the threshold the cited research actually tested. Converting once, at each testing event, keeps every phase's percentage prescriptions correctly calibrated against the evidence behind them.

**Weighted pull-ups use total system load.** For a weighted pull-up the athlete moves bodyweight plus whatever is on the belt or vest, so the e1RM is taken on that total: (bodyweight + added weight at the 5RM) ÷ 0.87, bodyweight is recorded at each test, and the weekly prescribed load is the percentage of that total minus current bodyweight (bodyweight only if the result is zero or negative). Applying the percentages to the added weight alone would have put early-phase sets near the athlete's tested total load.

**Rating of Perceived Exertion (RPE).** RPE is a subjective 1–10 scale an athlete uses to self-rate how hard a set felt, based on how many more reps they believe they could have done before failure:

| RPE | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 10 | Max effort — could not have done another rep |
| 8–9 | 1–2 reps left in the tank |
| 6–7 | Moderate-hard, several reps left, form still clean |
| 3–5 | Light to moderate — technique work and acclimation sessions |

RPE is a load-management tool, not a replacement for the %e1RM prescriptions that drive most of the program's actual training — fixed percentages exist precisely so load doesn't drift week to week on a subjective scale. RPE governs the places a fixed percentage doesn't yet apply: novice/onboarding technique work, pre-testing acclimation sessions, the RPE 7–8 top set for athletes without four re-entry workouts (Section 4), and Phase 5's session-load tracking below. Where this program caps something at "RPE 5–6," that is a deliberate ceiling keeping the work well short of a working set.

**Session-RPE (sRPE) for in-season load tracking.** In Phase 5, each athlete rates every practice, lift, and game on the same 0–10 scale (Borg CR-10), and that rating is multiplied by session duration to produce a session load. Summed across a week (acute load) and compared against a rolling four-week average (chronic load), this produces an acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR) used to flag weeks of elevated injury risk — see Section 8 and Section 9 for the full mechanics and its limitations.

## 3. Phase 0 — Transition & Pre-Testing Prep

Phase 0 begins the Monday after the roster's actual final game and runs through the Sunday immediately before Phase 1's Testing Week, whatever those dates turn out to be in a given year — this is anchored to the real schedule, not a fixed calendar date, because season length varies with playoff results. For the 2026 season, that places Phase 0's start at Monday, October 26 (or November 2 if a consolation game extends the season), running through Sunday, December 13, 2026. That is 6 or 7 whole calendar weeks; the gap from the final game itself to Testing Week is 6.4–7.4 weeks, because the game falls partway through its week.

That window is not treated uniformly. The **first 1–2 weeks** are true active recovery: physical and mental recovery after the season, injury assessment and rehab as needed, no formal training load and no expectation of any kind. This is the part general periodization literature (Bompa's framework; the NSCA's CSCS periodization chapter) actually supports — a short active-rest transition between the competitive season and the next preparatory block.

The **remaining weeks** (roughly four to five most years) run the **Pre-Testing Prep Sessions**: a real, coach-facilitated, attendance-optional program — nine sessions, Tuesday/Thursday, anchored to the district's actual November–December calendar — rather than an unstructured "stay active" placeholder. Attendance does not affect roster status or playing time, the same voluntary framing Phase 3 uses for its own pre-Testing-Window acclimation sessions, but the sessions themselves are programmed and coach-run. Because attendance is optional, an athlete who skips the final-week sessions does not test cold: Phase 1's readiness rule has them run the movement screen on Testing Week's first day and tests a lift only after the coach signs off technique on it, and an athlete with fewer than four attended Prep sessions does not take a heavy 5RM at all in Testing Week (Section 4). The five-week arc solves two goals at once: athletes coming off a six-plus-week layoff need a genuine, unhurried ramp back into training (per the CSCCa/NSCA transition-period guidelines discussed in Section 9), while also needing to arrive at Testing Week able to produce a real, representative 5RM rather than a pre-fatigued or informally-maxed one. The sessions start at pure bodyweight and general movement, add barbell work only as light technique re-familiarization (never past RPE 5–6, never a tested max), and taper back down to a brief movement screen in the week immediately before Testing Week — which doubles as this boundary's required pre-max-testing acclimation window. Every session opens with the NMT warm-up in the trimmed form Phase 1 uses (Section 9), re-establishing that habit before Phase 1 proper begins.

This is not an on-ramp for incoming freshmen. An incoming eighth-grader is not eligible to join until their own school year ends, which lands them at Phase 3's Testing Window (mid-to-late June) — roughly six months after Phase 0 has already run its course. Their actual entry point is Phase 3's first-time-athlete path (Section 6).

## 4. Phase 1 — Winter: General Prep / Max Strength & Hypertrophy

**Intent.** Build the raw strength and muscle-mass foundation that later phases convert into speed and power — the General Physical Preparedness (GPP) block.

**Research backing.** The NSCA's Youth Resistance Training position statement (Faigenbaum et al., *Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research*, 2009) and the ASCA's companion Position Stand both confirm that properly supervised resistance training is safe and effective for high-school-age athletes, with technique mastery and progressive overload as the gating factors for adding load — not chronological age or grade level. The NSCA's broader Long-Term Athletic Development position statement frames a winter spent building a general strength base as an investment in multi-year development, not a shortcut to rush past on the way to sport-specific work. This program applies that guidance as a **technique-gated, not age-gated**, readiness standard: freshmen with real training age train at near-adult intensity once they demonstrate competent technique under load, consistent with Jeffreys' multi-year high-school periodization model.

Squat strength carries real, well-supported durability value: Case, Knudson & Downey (2020, *Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research*) found Division I collegiate athletes (football, volleyball, softball; n=71) with lower relative back-squat strength had significantly higher rates of in-season lower-extremity injury (g=0.85–0.86), with elevated risk below roughly 2.2× bodyweight (men) or 1.6× bodyweight (women). Its transfer to sprint and change-of-direction performance is a less settled claim: Wisløff et al. (2004, *British Journal of Sports Medicine*) found a strong correlation between half-squat 1RM and sprint/vertical-jump performance in elite soccer players, but a larger, more recent study (Loturco et al., 2018, *Frontiers in Physiology*, n=303 elite team-sport athletes) found bar-power output was a better predictor of acceleration, speed, and jump performance than 1RM strength alone. That split is exactly why this program pairs a strength-focused phase (Phase 1) with a dedicated power/bar-speed phase (Phase 2, CAT and jump-family training) rather than assuming strength alone converts to speed. All three cited studies are adult, non-high-school populations — a real gap in the literature, stated here rather than left implicit.

**Load and effort structure.** Main lifts (back squat, front squat, bench press, deadlift/RDL, overhead press, pull-up/row) run 4 sets × 5 reps at 75–85% of e1RM across an 8-week block, with a flat 65–70% e1RM back-off set (10–12 reps, controlled tempo) supplying the hypertrophy stimulus a pure 4×5 strength scheme does not. Weeks 2, 4 and 8 run a scheduled volume dip — 3 sets instead of 4, same intensity. Week 2 is the first training week after Winter Break (Testing Week ends Dec 18; school resumes Jan 4) and reuses this mechanism rather than resuming cold at full prescribed load; Weeks 4 and 8 sit immediately before each block's peak week. The dip is an unconditional, calendar-driven fatigue-management measure that does not depend on any athlete missing a rep; auto-regulation (drop load 5–10% if prescribed reps aren't achievable) and the Week 6 retest's naturally lower-volume structure handle uneven, individual fatigue. Weeks 5 and 9 — each block's peak intensity week — run 4×4 at 85% e1RM rather than 4×5, landing inside Prilepin's Chart's 2–4 rep/set guideline for that intensity zone rather than grinding a near-maximal fifth rep on heavy, spinal-loaded lifts. **Exception: barbell overhead press runs 3×4 at 85% e1RM in Weeks 5 and 9, not 4×4.** **Lineman load bias:** the position bias is ±2.5 percentage points around the prescribed percentage, and in Weeks 5 and 9 the lineman ceiling is 87% of e1RM, not 87.5% — because e1RM is the 5RM divided by 0.87, 87% is exactly the tested 5RM load, and repeated sets of four above what an athlete showed for one set of five are not supported by the test.

**Testing Week layout.** Monday squat, Tuesday bench press and pull-up, Thursday deadlift, Friday overhead press and make-ups. The two heavy lower-body tests sit about 72 hours apart with an upper-body day between them, so the deadlift baseline isn't taken on squat fatigue; a missed lower-body test is made up on Friday only if the other lower test was at least 48 hours earlier, otherwise at the start of Week 2. **Four-workout re-entry rule:** the Inter-Association Task Force's transitional period (Section 9: the first 7-10 days, at minimum the first four separate-day workouts, of progressive volume and intensity) is applied as no heavy 5RM before four attended non-maximal workouts, and the Pre-Testing Prep sessions are how athletes meet it. An athlete with fewer than four attended sessions works up to one top set of five at RPE 7–8 instead (a provisional, deliberately conservative e1RM) and takes a real 5RM at the Week 6 retest or later.

**Injury prevention woven into every session** (see Section 9 for full detail): a trimmed FIFA 11+-style NMT warm-up runs before every lift session (the full version in the field phases); the Nordic hamstring curl runs twice a week, after the lift, on Day B and Day D only in Phases 1–2 (Phases 3–4 use Day A and Day C, after the session), and the lateral bound is sequenced post-session on squat/hinge days to avoid pre-fatiguing the muscles those lifts need; a self-resisted 4-way neck isometric protocol is kept as low-risk physical preparation; and a shoulder-health finisher offsets the phase's heavy pressing volume. A next-day readiness rule governs the squat-Monday/hinge-Tuesday pairing, and stop-and-hand-off rules (concussion, injury or illness, persistent pain) apply in every phase (Section 9).

**Novice/Technique Onboarding Track.** A true first-time lifter — a mid-year first-timer already enrolled at the high school, a late transfer, or a returning athlete flagged on the Testing Week movement screen — completes a 3-week, RPE-based (6–7) dumbbell/goblet/bodyweight track across the same four movement patterns before testing a barbell 5RM, with a coach sign-off checklist gating graduation. This is a floor, not a ceiling: an athlete who isn't clean and controlled across all four patterns at the end of Week 3 continues the track rather than being pushed into Testing Week on a calendar deadline. Incoming freshmen are not this track's primary population — their on-ramp is Phase 3's equivalent (Section 6) — but the track remains in place for the narrower population that does arrive here without a training base.

**Multi-Sport Maintenance Track.** Any athlete whose winter-sport commitments (basketball, wrestling) conflict with two or more of the four weekly lifting slots runs a 2-day/week track instead: main-lift intensity identical to the full track's Progression Scheme, accessory circuit cut entirely, Nordic curl (only when the two track days are 48+ hours apart, otherwise on the hinge day alone) and shoulder-health work unchanged. This directly applies the finding (Hoffman & Kang; see Section 7) that intensity, not volume or frequency, drives strength retention — a multi-sport athlete's other-sport training is already supplying substantial load, so the accessory circuit, not the main lift's intensity, is the lower-priority piece to cut. A light dumbbell Overhead Press touch is included so overhead-pressing capacity isn't completely untrained for the phase, with a barbell technique re-familiarization touch the week before each barbell retest.

**Calendar.** Testing Week runs Monday, December 14 – Friday, December 18, 2026, timed to land after Phase 0's window and bank real training weeks before Winter Break rather than testing maxes days before the closure. Weeks 2–9 run through February 26, 2027. Winter Break (the district's Dec 24–31 entry is eight days, and with its separate Jan 1 entry that is nine consecutive closure dates; December 21–23 is deliberately left unprogrammed) is a scheduled no-training gap; Week 2 (the first week back) runs the same 3-set volume-dip mechanism used at Weeks 4 and 8 rather than resuming cold at full prescribed load. District closures that fall on a training day (MLK Day, Presidents' Day) and a Staff In-Service day (Week 7) each close a Monday. In those weeks (4, 7 and 8) Day A (Back Squat) moves to Tuesday and Day B (Hinge) to Wednesday, so no session is dropped and the squat-then-hinge order is unchanged.

**Pre-testing acclimation standard.** Because Testing Week follows a genuine multi-week layoff, the program applies its standing transition-period rule here: informal, optional acclimation touches (light movement, no loaded testing) are offered in the days before any Testing Week, rather than testing cold on day one. This standard, established here and at the Phase 2-to-Phase 3 boundary, is applied throughout the program wherever a real gap in training precedes a maximal-effort test.

## 5. Phase 2 — Spring: Strength-Speed & Power

**Intent.** Convert the strength base built in winter into explosive, fast force production — the Specific Physical Preparedness (SPP) block that most directly builds what football demands.

**Research backing.** Both plyometric training and strength training independently improve sprint and change-of-direction performance in adolescent athletes (a 2025 systematic review/meta-analysis on male adolescent team-sport athletes, *BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation*), supporting this phase's use of both rather than either alone. Bar speed matters as much as bar weight: Loturco et al. found the jump squat produced a significantly larger transfer to sprint speed than the Olympic push press in elite young soccer players, and separate research on 300+ elite team-sport athletes found both maximum strength and bar-power output independently predicted sprint/COD performance — meaning this phase needs a heavy-strength lane and a fast-bar-speed lane, not one or the other.

**Compensatory Acceleration Training (CAT)** — submaximal loads (50–70% e1RM) moved with maximal intended bar speed through the full range of motion — is introduced here as the phase's headline new stimulus, deliberately held back from Phase 1 so it lands as a genuinely new coaching cue. Its strongest backing is football-specific: Jones, Hunter, Fleisig, Escamilla & Lemak (1999, *Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research*) had NCAA Division 1AA football players train upper-body CAT-style and improve bench press more than a conventional-velocity control group (+9.85 kg vs. +5.00 kg; the abstract does not report duration or loads), and a 2014 study of 24 collegiate baseball players reporting an 11.7% bench increase over 5 weeks of CAT with bands or chains, with no control group. Both studies are collegiate rather than high-school samples, and the 1999 study is a single, now-decades-old trial — the bench-press difference describes that one trial's outcome, not a guaranteed effect size, though the underlying mechanism (maximal intended bar speed on submaximal load) is well-established training theory beyond that one study.

**Structure: Strength Lane + Power Lane.** Each of the four weekly days runs a Strength Lane (3 sets at a climbing percentage of e1RM) followed by a Power Lane exercise at fixed, lighter loads moved for maximal speed — Trap Bar Jump Squat and Trap Bar Jump Shrug (30–40% e1RM), CAT Bench Press (50–70% e1RM), and Landmine Rotational Press or Medicine Ball Rotational Throw. The **trap bar jump shrug replaces the hang clean**: Suchomel & Sole (2017, *Journal of Sports Science & Medicine*) directly compared the two and found the jump shrug produced significantly greater relative peak power at every load tested (d = 2.53) than the hang power clean achieved even at its own optimal load, with no catch position to coach — a better result on the quality the exercise exists to build, with less coaching risk, for a squad with only two coaches during the school year. **Loaded jump-family work (jump squat, jump shrug) is gated behind a coach-observed, unloaded landing assessment that every athlete — linemen included — takes in Testing Week:** three low-box jump-and-stick landings and three broad-jump landings, recorded pass or defer. Phase 1's jump-station work reaches skill positions only, so it can't serve as the gate for everyone. This is a behavioral, coach-observable standard rather than a clinical one, with criteria that are coach-set conventions; an athlete who defers, or any true first-year novice, runs the same slot unloaded (Countermovement Jump or Medicine Ball Scoop Toss) and is re-assessed every two weeks. Loaded jump sets also need a coach looking directly at that athlete for the whole set — the two-rack offset in the room design reduces simultaneous live reps but isn't a guarantee of continuous supervision — so they run one athlete at a time when needed.

**Calendar.** Testing Week runs March 1–5, 2027, immediately following Phase 1's close — there is no transition-period gap here, since Phase 2 starts right where Phase 1 ends. Weeks 2–11 run through May 21, 2027. Spring Break (Friday, March 26 – Friday, April 2, 2027; school resumes April 5) falls mid-progression; the week immediately following it runs at a reduced 78% e1RM for 3 reps (not the mid-progression 84%×4 the calendar position would otherwise call for) — both intensity and volume trimmed for that one week, reusing the same "conservative restart" figure Phase 1 uses after its own retest, since an 8-day full layoff is a materially different situation than the single-day gaps Phase 1's built-in dip weeks absorb. Testing Week uses the same layout as Phase 1 (Monday vertical jump and squat, Tuesday bench and pull-up, Thursday deadlift, Friday overhead press and make-ups).

## Phase 2–3 Bridge

Phase 2 closes May 21, 2027, but Phase 3's Testing Window doesn't open until June 21 — roughly four and a half calendar weeks with no structured session, well past the threshold that triggers this program's transition-period guidance. Rather than leave that gap as an informal, optional stopgap, the existing Multi-Sport Maintenance Track continues — same 2-day/week structure, same intensity, held at Week 11's load rather than progressing further — on a Tuesday/Friday pattern from May 25 through June 15, 2027, leaving a short, unavoidable six-day gap before Testing Window.

**One session carries a re-entry ramp: the bridge's two most reliable sessions, May 25 and June 4, sit 10 days apart once its two contingent bonus dates are discounted, so June 4 runs at 78% e1RM rather than the full Week 11 load — holding peak load across that internal gap would have recreated, inside the bridge, the exact cold-start-at-high-load scenario it exists to prevent.**

This is framed as transition-period/cold-start safety ahead of a true max-effort retest, not as protecting speed or power qualities from decline — the sprint/power-specific detraining evidence (Bissas et al.: three weeks of complete cessation after a six-week block retained 98.7% of performance) is considerably weaker than the strength-maintenance case this bridge's maintenance dose otherwise rests on (Bickel, Cross & Bamman, 2011).

Phase 3's own larger training system (4+ coaches, a 30–40 athlete roster, sled/field equipment) is tied to the school year ending, not a date that could simply move earlier — making Phase 2's own small-scale track, not an extension of Phase 3's, the realistic place for this bridge to live.

## 6. Phase 3 — Early Summer: Speed & Conditioning

**Intent.** Pure speed mechanics and work capacity, timed for when athletes have full days free after school lets out.

**Research backing.** Resisted sled sprinting has direct, high-school-specific evidence: a 2020 study (*Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research*) on 53 male high-school athletes found the heaviest tested sled-pull loads (133% bodyweight) produced the greatest gains in horizontal force production and 0–10m/0–20m acceleration; a companion sled-push study on 50 high-school athletes (Cahill et al.) found all three resisted groups improved their 5–20m split times significantly while the unresisted group did not, with the largest gains in the heavy group and over the first 5m (per the published abstract; split-by-split results were not checked). It is cited as corroborating evidence that heavy sled loading works in this age group, not because sled pushing is programmed here: Phase 3 uses sled pulls only. This program hedges rather than bets the whole phase on resisted work alone — the evidence on resisted sprint training's advantage over unresisted sprinting is genuinely mixed across recent meta-analyses — by pairing every heavy sled session with unresisted acceleration sprints in the same session, a direct, structural guard against grooving altered, forward-leaning "ground-plowing" mechanics. Conditioning runs as sprint interval training (SIT) rather than steady-state work: a 2025–2026 systematic review/meta-analysis on adolescents found SIT significantly improves both aerobic and anaerobic capacity, and short maximal efforts fit the practical demands of July heat with a squad not yet in-season-motivated better than long steady-state running does.

**Testing Window** runs Monday–Tuesday, June 21–22, 2027 — after, not on, the district's graduation day/last day of school — split across two days specifically so shuttle-run fatigue doesn't contaminate the sprint numbers that drive Day A's sled-load calibration. A roughly four-and-a-half-week gap separates the end of Phase 2 and this window every year; it's now closed by Phase 2's own Phase 2–3 Bridge (see the Phase 2–3 Bridge tab) rather than left as an informal stopgap, down to a short six-day unprogrammed stretch right before Testing Window itself.

**Sprint runway for first-timers.** Phases 1–2 give athletes only build-up sprints inside the trimmed warm-up, so a first-time athlete (or any athlete without a recent sprint runway) meets maximal-effort sprinting at Testing Window with little graded exposure. The Thursday, June 24 session is therefore used to give those athletes a short progressive sprint runway and the shuttle before sled loading is calibrated.

**Day D (Maintenance Lift)** runs once weekly, upper-body focused (Bench Press, Pull-up, Overhead Press at ~80% of each athlete's most recently tested e1RM, plus a light 2×5 @ ~60% e1RM Squat/Deadlift maintenance touch for returning athletes) — holding the strength built across Phases 1–2 without competing for recovery with the phase's real training stimulus (sled work, plyometrics, sprinting), which is already substantial lower-body loading that touches the upper body not at all. **For the weighted pull-up, "~80%" applies to the total-system-load e1RM (bodyweight plus added weight; Section 2), and the belt load is that figure minus current bodyweight**. **Day C's SIT conditioning template is also what camp's end-of-practice conditioning formalizes onto once two-a-days begin** (see the Camp Bridge tab) — the same 20m shuttle format and linemen recovery bias, continuing onto the same field rather than a separate method built for camp.

**First-time athlete on-ramp.** Incoming freshmen enter the program here, not in Phase 1 — they become eligible only once their own school year ends, landing them at this Testing Window rather than Phase 1's December start. A first-time athlete completes a movement screen at Testing Window, then two weeks of RPE-based (6–7) technique work on Dumbbell Bench Press, Inverted Row, and Dumbbell Overhead Press before a first real 5RM test in Week 3 — one clean technique session is sufficient runway for these three movements, since none carries axial spinal-loading risk. **Squat and Deadlift run on a longer, separate runway**: because these movements carry real valgus-collapse and spinal-flexion risk under a still-developing lifter's stabilization, they require three RPE-gated technique sessions (Weeks 2, 3, and 4) on Goblet Squat and Dumbbell Romanian Deadlift — matching the three-week floor Phase 1's own Novice Track sets for the same movement patterns — before any loaded test. The Squat 5RM test itself runs in Phase 4's Week 1, Day D and the Deadlift 5RM test in Week 2, Day D (a week apart, never in one session), once those three sessions are banked, with a light touch on the other lower-body lift in each session so a first-timer isn't left with a single loaded exposure per lift heading into Phase 5. A graduated late-arrival policy (Testing Window on time; a short slip before Week 2; mid-phase; after Phase 3 ends; after Phase 4 ends) governs athletes who arrive off this schedule, always deferring Squat/Deadlift to whichever later point allows the same three-session floor, and stating plainly that an athlete joining very late enters the season without a real strength base — the program's job at that point is making sure they are never loaded against a number that was never measured, not pretending a few catch-up sessions close a six-month gap. **Late arrivals also meet maximal-effort sprinting without the team's prior exposure:** an athlete who joins after the Testing Window gets an individual, graded sprint exposure (progressive runs, then the shuttle) before any sled loading or SIT, rather than being dropped into the team's current week. As written, the first-timer's bench, row and overhead-press 5RM comes after one loaded RPE technique session (Week 2) plus the unloaded movement screen and a ramped, coach-watched test (Week 3: stop at the first technique breakdown and repeat Week 2 work for that lift). That is the program's own convention, not an evidence-based minimum, and the runway is thin; the Squat/Deadlift runway is the longer one. First-timers are treated as having no sprint runway by default: timed sprints wait for their first Day A and the shuttle moves to Thursday, June 24, and Part 3 of the NMT is graded (build-ups about 70–80%, bounding at moderate effort, plant-and-cut at half speed) until two clean exposures.

**Offense/defense practice-day assignment and its CNS-load reasoning.** A football-practice segment (install/air on offense days, 7v7 on defense days) runs immediately after every training session in this phase, with only a short break and no separate warm-up of its own. **Monday (Day A, heavy sled/max-velocity work) and Thursday (Day C, plyometrics/SIT conditioning) — this phase's two hardest sessions — carry the lower-demand offense install/air work; Tuesday (Day B, tempo/skills) and Wednesday (Day D, upper-body maintenance lift) — the two lightest sessions — carry 7v7.** This protects the phase's own 48+-hour CNS-recovery spacing between its highest-demand days, and keeps 7v7's reactive cutting and repeated-sprint demand off the days that already carry the week's heaviest CNS load; the NMT research behind this program's injury-prevention layer identifies fatigued neuromuscular control as a real ACL-risk factor, which is exactly the scenario of running 7v7 immediately after a fatiguing lift/conditioning session with no re-warm-up. A 5-minute reactivation block (reactive shuffle-and-cut work, a mirror drill, unloaded deceleration reps) runs immediately before the practice segment on the two defense days specifically, closing that fatigue-then-cutting gap without meaningfully cutting into practice time. This assignment puts the week's two 7v7 days back-to-back rather than spread through the week — a real, smaller trade-off worth watching (cumulative lower-body and connective-tissue load two days straight) against the larger risk it avoids.

**Heat & Hydration Checklist.** NJSIAA's WBGT (Wet Bulb Globe Temperature) Heat Participation Policy applies to this program's own outdoor sessions directly, year-round — not only to camp's preseason acclimatization window. An **on-site WBGT reading with a scientifically reliable device** is taken 30 minutes before every outdoor session and at least hourly during it, by the athletic trainer or a coach/designee appointed by the AD, and recorded on NJSIAA's Record Chart. A phone's stock heat-index reading is not a substitute, since heat index omits solar radiation, wind, and sun angle. Free forecast products (the NWS National Digital Forecast Database WBGT product, perryweather.com) are modeled regional data, cannot see a specific field's microclimate (especially turf surface heat), and are **not** a compliant substitute for the on-site reading; they are planning aids only. If no device is available, the session is not policy-compliant as run: the AD/athletic trainer is asked to supply one, and in the meantime any forecast of 80.0°F WBGT or higher is treated as at least Orange-tier, with indoor/modified work at Red-tier or higher. On Wednesday the Day D lift is indoors but the defense practice after it is outdoors, so the reading is taken 30 minutes before that practice. The policy's tiers govern the **full on-field day**, lift/conditioning plus the practice segment that follows, not just the training portion in isolation:

| WBGT | Flag | Requirement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Under 80.0°F | Green | Normal activity; 3 rest breaks/hour, 3 min each |
| 80.0–85.0°F | Yellow | Coach discretion on intense/prolonged work; 3 breaks/hour, 4 min each |
| 85.1–88.0°F | Orange | Max 2-hour full day; 4 breaks/hour, 4 min each; no helmets or shoulder pads |
| 88.1–90.0°F | Red | Max 1-hour full day with 20 min of rest spread across it; no conditioning work of any kind; no protective equipment |
| Over 90.0°F | Black | No outdoor workouts |

**Red means no conditioning of any kind.** The policy's Red-tier restriction is "no conditioning work," and the program reads that literally: no sled, SIT, tempo running or conditioning-style movement, indoors or out. A Red day is a lift-and-mobility day indoors, and the indoor warm-up is NMT Part 2 plus mobility only: no build-up sprints, bounding or cutting (Parts 1 and 3) and no Nordic.

**Emergency readiness is a checklist item, not an assumption.** NJSIAA's cold-water-immersion policy sets these on-field expectations (confirm the current wording with the AD): a shaded rest site; ice towels or ice-water spray above 85°F WBGT; a cold-water immersion tub or tarp (water under 60°F) reachable within 5–10 minutes at 80.0°F WBGT and above, with alternative cooling (ice, towels, shade) below that; a written emergency action plan that covers heat injury; and "cool first, transport second" for suspected exertional heat stroke — cooling starts where the athlete is, and with no athletic trainer on site a coach calls 911 and starts cooling immediately. The EAP itself is owned by the AD and athletic trainer. The policy copy reviewed contained no AED requirement, and none is stated here.

**Air quality.** The policy language reviewed contains no air-quality check. Phases 3 and 4 add one *recommended* (not required) AQI check by whoever takes the WBGT reading, with the athletic trainer or head coach authorized to move, shorten or cancel work, and no separate threshold of this program's own; EPA/AirNow activity guidance was not verified.

Anyone showing dizziness, nausea, confusion, or skin that's hot/dry rather than sweaty stops immediately and is moved to shade/AC for evaluation.

## 7. Phase 4 — Pre-Camp Taper

**Intent.** Arrive at the pre-camp blackout week — and then camp — fresh, not worn down. Volume drops sharply while intensity and bar/movement speed stay high, so the CNS stays primed rather than simply resting, following Welbourn's own "boiling point, not breaking point" principle.

**Research backing.** A 2020 review of tapering practices for powerlifting performance (Travis, Mujika, Gentles, Stone & Bazyler, *Sports*) associated the best strength/power outcomes with a taper of about two weeks and a 30–50% volume-load cut while holding at least 85% of tested 1RM; cuts larger than that (50–70%) showed no additional benefit and may work against it. Its evidence base is small and drawn from adult strength athletes, and it discusses longer tapers too, so it does not establish two weeks as a maximum - two weeks is this program's coaching choice, and the evidence doesn't establish a need for a third week. A companion study (Travis, Zwetsloot, Mujika, Stone & Bazyler, 2021, *Frontiers in Physiology*; 16 adult powerlifters) compared a one-week step taper with a three-week exponential taper (a steadily decreasing volume curve): muscle-fiber size increased significantly only after the step taper, squat-jump peak power improved in both groups, and the authors suggested the exponential model may favor neuromuscular performance. Because the tapers differed in length as well as shape, it is suggestive, not conclusive. Since this phase's priority is explosive readiness for camp, its volume curve borrows the exponential shape, and its cuts are deliberately uneven: plyometric volume stays closest to Phase 3 levels, because plyometric output is the kind of power quality that study points toward, while tempo runs, the skills circuit, and SIT conditioning — the highest-volume, lowest-specificity work — absorb most of the cut, with SIT dropped entirely in Week 2 to preserve 48+ hours of CNS-recovery spacing before camp. Both source studies are drawn from competitive powerlifters rather than team-sport or adolescent athletes — a real population gap worth naming specifically: a powerlifter tapers toward a single-day, low-volume, maximum-arousal meet with no competing metabolic or sport-skill demand, while this program's athletes taper the lift alongside concurrently-tapering field conditioning, then head straight into camp's heat and multi-directional field demand. That gap doesn't change the taper structure — Phase 4 already tapers its other modalities alongside the lift rather than holding them constant — but it means the "85% 1RM, 30–50% volume cut" figures are a starting template validated on a simpler case, not a number to apply rigidly against a coach's own read of an athlete carrying heavy accumulated field fatigue.

**Structure.** Week 1's Day A runs a single heavy-but-low-volume sled touch (90–100% bodyweight, 3×10m: %BW is an imprecise intensity proxy, so the load is kept modest and the technique check does the gating) — still a genuine step up from Phase 3's own 80-90% ceiling, closing out the sled progression in the direction the evidence points while staying consistent with a taper's job (intensity maintained, volume cut) and gated by an explicit technique-quality check rather than the %BW number alone. The Day D lift holds Phase 3's dose in Week 1 (3×5 @ ~80% e1RM) and cuts to 2×5 @ ~75% e1RM in Week 2 — cutting sets before cutting load, landing inside the volume-reduction range the Travis et al. review reported while keeping intensity below that review's ≥85% guidance by deliberate coaching judgment (e1RM is an estimate, the athletes are adolescents, and the practice segment still runs at full Week 1 intensity) — an evidence-informed extrapolation, not a validated dose. The weighted pull-up follows the same percentages applied to total-system-load e1RM (Section 2). Injury-prevention work (NMT, Nordic curl, shoulder-health finisher) does not taper at all: cutting it immediately before the highest-injury-risk period of the year (camp, then a full contact season) would undercut exactly what three phases of consistent dosing were meant to protect, and its own mechanical load is low enough that it doesn't compete with the taper's actual goal. Phase 4 keeps the full three-part NMT warm-up and the Nordic dose (2 sets of 8–10, twice a week, post-session on Day A and Day C only).

**Why the offense/defense practice segment does not taper in Week 2, even though the barbell lift does.** Phase 4's Week 2 ends on the last Monday–Thursday training week this program's cadence can fit before the estimated blackout week begins, and the blackout week itself is a full seven days of zero coach-led training immediately after that, before camp. That is roughly eleven days of sharply reduced-to-zero organized training between the end of Phase 4 and camp — closer to the recovery period the taper research is protecting than to an immediate loaded week before an event. Cutting the practice segment's own volume in Week 2 would not buy additional recovery the calendar isn't already providing; it would only cost preparation reps that matter given live 7v7s on the schedule. The barbell lift keeps its designed taper because it targets strength retention through a distinct, independently-evidenced mechanism the calendar gap does not substitute for — the two pieces are doing different jobs, and only one of them needs the calendar's help. The Monday/Thursday-offense, Tuesday/Wednesday-defense assignment and the pre-practice reactivation block carry forward unchanged from Phase 3, for the same reasoning, mattering here with even less margin for error since fewer days remain to recover from a bad pairing before blackout week. For the same reason Week 2's Friday (July 30) takes no makeups: a missed Week 2 session is simply missed.

**First-time athlete Squat/Deadlift testing.** The Squat 5RM test runs on Week 1's Day D and the Deadlift 5RM test on Week 2's Day D - the designed home, not a fallback, for every first-time athlete once Phase 3's three-session technique runway is banked. The two tests are a week apart and never share a session, matching Phase 1's testing layout (the deadlift test about 72 hours after the squat test, with at least 48 hours required). On each test day the tested lift goes first with the full testing ramp, the rest of Day D runs as written from the athlete's Phase 3 Week 3 numbers, and the other lower-body lift gets a light RPE 6 touch instead (DB RDL in Week 1, Goblet Squat in Week 2), so a first-timer enters Phase 5's in-season lifting with a tested number plus one light exposure per lift, not a single isolated test standing alone. The cost of the split is a first-timers-only Deadlift test inside the taper week.

## Camp Bridge

Between Phase 4's last session and Phase 5's Week 1 sits a full no-contact blackout week and then camp itself — three-plus weeks that would otherwise carry no lifting guidance at all, longer than the minimum-effective-dose research says a roster can go without a stimulus before real detraining sets in (Bickel, Cross & Bamman, 2011, *Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise*: training once a week at roughly half the prior volume-load fully preserved strength and muscle size over an eight-week reduced-training period, while complete cessation did not).

**Lifting.** No lifting runs during the first five days of NJSIAA's 14-day heat-acclimatization ramp — single practice per day, capped at three hours, the highest-risk window of the year for exertional illness, and a window where NATA's own guidelines count weight-room time against that same capped practice-time budget. Once two-a-day sessions begin, a once-a-week continuation of Phase 4 Week 2's taper-lift dose (Bench Press, Pull-up, Overhead Press; 2×5 @ ~75% e1RM, pull-up on total-system-load e1RM) bridges the gap through to the season opener; **Squat and Deadlift carry their own light maintenance touch through this bridge as well (2×5 @ ~60% e1RM)**, continuing from Phase 3 and Phase 4's Day D, so neither lift goes untrained at real intensity for three-plus months. Phase 5's GD-4/GD-2 runs a Week 1-2 re-entry ramp (70% then 78% e1RM, full 80-85% from Week 3) rather than loading straight into the season at full intensity off that stale number.

**Conditioning.** Conditioning at the end of camp practice is not a gap this program adds to: it stays built into the existing practice window, exactly as it has run at this program for more than a decade, which already satisfies NATA's practice-time structure (conditioning counts as part of total practice time, not an addition to it). **Named explicitly rather than left generic: this segment runs on Phase 3's own SIT conditioning template** — repeated maximal-effort 20m out-and-back shuttle sprints, the same format and linemen recovery bias Phase 3 already trains — continuing onto the field this roster has already been conditioning on for a month by the time camp opens, with volume set by the day of the acclimatization ramp rather than by Phase 3's calendar weeks or by whatever time practice leaves. Against the staff's typical ~10-minute end-of-practice allotment (not a hard ceiling — practice runs a scheduled 2.5 hours, often finishing around 2, well inside NJSIAA's 3-hour single-practice cap), Phase 3's own 2-set structure (30 sec between reps, ~3 min between sets, +25% for linemen) runs at full volume from Day 6 of the ramp for every position group, linemen's full 2×5 included — a few minutes past the typical 10 is not a real constraint given that schedule slack — and on a lighter ramp before that: 1 set of 4 reps on Days 1–2 and 2 sets of 4 reps on Days 3–5 (Phase 4 Week 1's and Phase 3 Week 2's own doses), at the same full recovery. The WBGT tier overrides all of it. The rule that doesn't flex is the recovery structure itself, regardless of how much time is available: never shorten it to fit more volume, which would work against the heat-illness research this section is built on; trimming linemen to 4 reps a set (never the recovery) is a fallback for a day genuinely running tight against the 3-hour ceiling, not a standing default. What the evidence refines, rather than reverses, is volume scaled down and recovery extended (+25%) for linemen specifically — who account for roughly 97% of documented high-school/college exertional-heat-stroke deaths (1998–2018), a physiological rather than conditioning-level difference — the heaviest-intensity version of it held back from Days 1–5 of the acclimatization ramp, which covers the first two to four days where essentially all such fatalities cluster, and the same WBGT-gated framework already governing Phase 3/4's outdoor work extended to camp, so an Orange/Red day shortens or cuts this segment first (National Federation of State High School Associations Sports Medicine Advisory Committee, Anderson et al., 2024, "Preventing Exertional Heat Stroke in Football: Time for a Paradigm Shift").

## 8. Phase 5 — In-Season (Maintenance)

**Intent.** Preserve the strength, power, and speed built across Phases 1–3 without adding meaningful training stress on top of what practice and games already demand. This is a maintenance phase, not a development phase.

**Structure: GD-4/GD-2.** Lifting drops to two days a week, labeled by distance from the nearest game (GD-4, GD-2, and so on) rather than fixed weekdays, since New Jersey high school games move between Thursday, Friday, and Saturday and a template pinned to specific weekdays would break the first week a game isn't on its usual day. The GD offsets are authoritative: a Friday game puts Lift Day 1 on Monday and Lift Day 2 on Wednesday; a Saturday game shifts both a day later (Tuesday and Thursday, with Monday practice only); a Thursday game has no Sunday session, so it runs one lift day (Squat + Bench on Monday), skips the Deadlift/Pull-up day and doesn't make it up. Each lift day runs two full-body main lifts (Squat + Bench on GD-4; Deadlift + Pull-up on GD-2) for 3 sets of 3–5 reps at 80–85% of each athlete's tested e1RM for that lift (the Phase 2 retest for returning athletes; for first-time athletes, the Phase 3 Week 3 test for Bench and Pull-up and the Phase 4 tests for Squat and Deadlift), moved at **"Heavy Maintenance" pace** — controlled and purposeful, but not labeled CAT (CAT stays defined at 50-70% e1RM elsewhere in this program, and real bar speed naturally slows well below that at 80-85% regardless of intent). For the weighted pull-up the percentage applies to total-system-load e1RM (~80%; the 2×5 bridge row ~75%) and the belt load is that figure minus bodyweight (Section 2). Football-specific evidence (Hoffman & Kang, 2003; 53 NCAA Division III players) found in-season athletes training at ≥80% of pre-season 1RM had significantly greater strength improvements than those training below that threshold, with volume and compliance not significantly related to the outcome — the closest research basis for holding intensity high while cutting frequency and volume, applied here to high-school athletes as an extrapolation. A 2021 review of the minimal dose needed to preserve strength (Spiering et al., *Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research*) points the same direction - strength can be maintained for up to 32 weeks on one session a week if relative load is kept, at least in younger populations - while noting there are insufficient data for specific recommendations to athletes. **Squat and Deadlift specifically ramp in over the season's first two weeks (70% e1RM, then 78%, full 80-85% from Week 3)** rather than loading straight in, since a returning athlete's e1RM is three-to-four months old by the opener even with the Camp Bridge's maintenance touch (above) keeping the motor pattern current, and a first-timer's fresher Phase 4 numbers get the same conservative re-entry after blackout week and camp; Bench Press and Pull-up, which never went dormant, start at full prescription.

**Why the two lift days sit early in the week, not right after a game.** A GPS-tracked study of in-season college football (Johnson, Yang, Cabarkapa et al., 2025) found that teams' own practice load is already highest four days out from the next game and lowest the day before it. This program's lift days sit on the two practice days furthest from the last game and the next one, working with that existing shape rather than stacking a maximal lift onto the 24–72-hour window when post-game muscle damage markers are still elevated and a team's own practice schedule is already treating those days as recovery-oriented.

**Why there is no dedicated mid-season retest.** Scheduling a maximal-effort testing day mid-season would add exactly the kind of avoidable near-maximal exertion this phase exists to minimize, purely to collect a number. Instead, the sRPE/ACWR load-tracking system (below) flags load spikes and overreaching athletes every week so a coach takes a look. It tracks perceived session difficulty and exposure, not strength, so it cannot detect a strength decline, and the program accepts that strength loss isn't directly measured in season; the one direct signal is a coach's observation that a top set at an unchanged weight has become slower, grindier, or missed reps, which gets the same hold-or-reduce response. Lift loads are set off each athlete's tested e1RM for that lift and held there unless the tracking data or a coach's read says otherwise.

**The sRPE/ACWR protocol.** Roughly 20–30 minutes after every practice, lift, and game, each athlete gives a single session-RPE (0–10, Borg CR-10). Session load = RPE × session duration; weekly (acute) load is the sum across the week; chronic load is a rolling four-week average; ACWR is acute ÷ chronic. A ratio of 0.8–1.3 is the "sweet spot" associated with the lowest injury risk; ≥1.5 is linked to substantially elevated injury risk across team sports (Gabbett, 2016, *British Journal of Sports Medicine*). Monotony (mean daily load ÷ standard deviation of daily loads) and strain (load × monotony) serve as a supplementary signal (Haddad, Stylianides, Djaoui, Dellal & Chamari, 2017) — a high-strain week (high load, low day-to-day variation) is flagged as risk even when ACWR alone looks fine. **ACWR is treated as a rough, easy-to-compute heuristic for a coach's attention, not a validated clinical predictor**: the ratio's mathematical structure has drawn real methodological criticism (Impellizzeri et al., 2020, 2021), since the acute week's load is also part of the chronic average it's divided by, which can produce coupling artifacts that look like signal even when they aren't. This program still uses it because it's simple enough for a two-person coaching staff to calculate and act on weekly, with the monotony/strain metrics as a second, differently-constructed check. An ACWR pushing toward or past 1.5, or a high-strain week, is the signal to hold or reduce lift loads that week; a quiet week is never, by itself, a reason to push harder — this remains a maintenance phase regardless of what a good week's data shows.

**Late-arriving first-time athletes.** An athlete joining during camp or after the season starts has no off-season e1RM for GD-4/GD-2 to load against. The football staff's own contact and conditioning ramp-up (governed by NJSIAA's heat-acclimatization mandate during camp, or ordinary coaching judgment once the season is underway) is not this program's call to make. This program's own, narrower commitment is that the athlete is never loaded against a percentage of a number that was never measured: they run RPE-based technique work in place of the barbell percentage prescriptions until a real 5RM test clears them, on the same differentiated runway used throughout the program — one clean technique session for Bench/Row/OHP, three for Squat/Deadlift, given the axial-loading risk those two movements carry. An athlete arriving this late is, realistically, likely to play before that testing and technique work is fully banked; that is a roster-management and player-safety judgment for the coaching and football staff together, and the program's honest framing is that no amount of catch-up work closes a genuine six-month training gap — its job is making sure the number on the bar always corresponds to something real.

## 9. Injury Prevention & Safety

**NMT warm-up.** A neuromuscular training warm-up built on the FIFA 11+ template, combining strength, balance/proprioception and plyometric work. Multicomponent NMT warm-ups reduce ACL injuries by roughly 51–62% and lower-limb injuries broadly by around 40% in youth sport (National Athletic Trainers' Association position statement; a 2017 systematic review/meta-analysis on multimodal injury-prevention programs), in studies of youth athletes (mostly soccer, mostly female). The effect for high-school American football, and for the trimmed warm-up used here, is not known. It works when it is done consistently, and a 10-minute version performed no differently from a 20-minute one. **What we do:** the full three-part warm-up (10 to 13 minutes) in Phases 3 and 4, the field speed, plyometric and conditioning phases. In the barbell phases (1, 2 and 5) it is trimmed to Part 2 (core, neck, balance, landing) plus two build-up sprints, about 5 minutes. The trimmed version is a coaching decision; it has not been tested in a trial.

**Nordic hamstring curl.** An eccentric hamstring exercise with the strongest evidence for preventing hamstring strains. van der Horst et al. (2015, *American Journal of Sports Medicine*), a 579-athlete RCT, found a roughly 68% reduction in injury risk, and a 2017 meta-analysis (Al Attar et al., *Sports Medicine*) confirmed it across five pooled studies. Both are adult soccer players; no trial in adolescent American football was found. A 2025 scoping review (Tedeschi, Giorgi & Donati; 12 studies, no meta-analysis or risk-of-bias assessment) concluded that combining sprint exposure with eccentric strengthening appears more effective than either alone, but most included studies measured proxies such as eccentric strength or sprint performance rather than injuries. An adolescent trial (Freeman et al., 2019; 28 athletes, mean age 16.2, Nordic versus sprint training, twice weekly for four weeks) measured eccentric strength and 40 m sprint time, not injuries, and showed small eccentric strength gains in both groups. Neither shows a measured injury reduction. **What we do:** 2 sets, twice a week, never on consecutive days. Phases 1–2 Day B and Day D after the lift; Phases 3–4 Day A (Monday) and Day C (Thursday) after the session, which keeps them about 72 hours apart; Phase 5 GD-4 and GD-2 after the lift. If a session is moved so the two would land within 48 hours of each other, only the first runs that week. Reps per set: 4–6 (Phase 1 weeks 1–3), 6–8 (weeks 4–6), 8–10 (week 7 on through Phase 4), 6–8 in season. This is a conservative coach-set dose, not a validated adolescent-football dose. More than mild next-day hamstring soreness, hamstring tightness while sprinting, or a visible drop in sprint speed means skip it and see the athletic trainer.

**Neck 4-way isometric hold.** A short, self-applied hold in each of four directions (front, back, each side), 6–8 seconds per direction, in the NMT warm-up. Collins et al. (2014) is an observational study of high-school soccer, basketball and lacrosse players, not football, and as reported found greater neck strength associated with lower concussion risk. An association is not proof that neck training prevents concussion, and that evidence remains insufficient. **What we do:** keep the hold because it is short, cheap and low-risk, not as a concussion-prevention claim. Pain-free, controlled isometrics only, self-applied (the athlete presses their own hand against their own head). Neck pain, or a recent neck or head injury, means the athletic trainer evaluates it first.

**Shoulder-health finisher.** Light, high-rep scapular stabilizer and rotator-cuff work (face pull or band pull-apart) to offset the program's heavy pressing volume, per standard clinical guidance (Reinold, Escamilla & Wilk, 2009, *Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy*). **What we do:** 2×15–20 after every session, at a light load. It does not progress in volume.

**Stop and hand off.** The program has no medical protocol of its own, and coaches do not diagnose or clear anyone. A suspected concussion means immediate removal, no same-day return, hand-off to the athletic trainer under Dover's concussion policy and the district's emergency action plan, and no lifting, sprinting, practice or games until the school's medical clearance and graded return are complete. Illness, injury or a medical restriction follows the athletic-trainer and preparticipation-exam process, with an individually adjusted return. New or persistent pain, including growth-spurt joint, heel, knee or back pain, means stop or modify the exercise, report it through the athletic trainer, and re-check technique before restoring load. An athlete with unusual soreness, pain or a visible drop in movement quality modifies or skips the next day's heavy lower-body work.

**Transition-period guidelines.** The Inter-Association Task Force's best-practice recommendations (Casa et al., 2012) define the first 7–10 days (at minimum the first four separate-day workouts) of any new conditioning cycle as a transitional period needing a written, progressive plan of volume, intensity and work-to-rest ratio. The CSCCa and NSCA Joint Consensus Guidelines for Transition Periods (Safe Return to Training Following Inactivity, 2019) set graduated workload reductions for the first weeks back. Exertional heat illness, exertional rhabdomyolysis and cardiorespiratory failure spike in the first two to four weeks after a return from inactivity. **What we do:** this governs the Phase 0-to-Phase 1 transition (including the four-workout re-entry rule at Testing Week, Section 4), the gap before Phase 3's Testing Window, and every first-time or late-arrival entry.

**Heat acclimatization.** NJSIAA mandates a 14-day preseason heat-acclimatization ramp: no more than one practice per day for the first five days, no single practice over three hours, a helmet as the only protective equipment on days one and two, helmets and shoulder pads only on days three to five, and all protective equipment and full contact not before day six. Roughly 6,500 high school football athletes are treated for exertional heat illness each year in the US. **What we do:** camp itself follows the football staff's schedule, outside this program. The program's part is to bring athletes to camp well conditioned (Phase 4's taper and the blackout week's timing) and to follow the WBGT policy in Phases 3 and 4 (Section 6).
